keyPoints: ["Both: cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into two daughter cells, starting during telophase.","Animal cell: cytokinesis by cleavage - membrane pinches inward at the middle.","Plant cell: cytokinesis by forming a new cell wall (cell plate) across the centre, because the rigid wall prevents pinching."]
modelAnswer: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that produces two separate daughter cells, and it starts while telophase is still in progress; its pattern differs between animal and plant cells because a plant cell has a rigid cell wall and an animal cell does not. In an animal cell, cytokinesis occurs by cleavage: the cell membrane pinches inward at the middle (forming a cleavage furrow) until it constricts all the way through, splitting the cell into two. In a plant cell, because the rigid cell wall prevents pinching, cytokinesis instead occurs by the formation of a new cell wall (a cell plate) that grows outward from the centre of the cell to the existing wall, dividing the cell into two.

modelAnswer: Meiosis II mirrors mitosis because both are equational: no pairing or crossing over precedes them, chromosomes line up singly on the equator, and sister chromatids separate to give cells retaining the same chromosome number as the starting cell. modelAnswer: Meiosis is a reduction division: it reduces the chromosome number of a diploid (2n) parent cell to half, producing haploid (n) daughter cells (gametes). When two haploid gametes, one from each parent, fuse at fertilization, the full diploid (2n) chromosome number is restored in the zygote. In this way meiosis prevents the chromosome number from doubling every generation and keeps it constant from one generation to the next.

keyPoints: ["Crossing over (meiosis I): exchanges DNA segments between homologous chromatids, creating new gene combinations.","Independent combination of chromosomes into gametes mixes maternal/paternal chromosomes differently each time.","Together these two events are the source of genetic variation in gametes and zygotes."]
modelAnswer: Meiosis produces new combinations of genes in the gametes, and hence in the zygote formed at fertilisation, through two key events. First, crossing over during meiosis I exchanges segments of DNA between homologous (non-sister) chromatids, producing chromatids with new gene combinations. Second, homologous chromosomes and their combinations are distributed independently into different gametes, so each gamete ends up with a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Together, crossing over and this independent chromosome combination are the two important events that give rise to genetic variation among offspring.
stem: How does meiosis contribute to genetic variations?

keyPoints: ["Maintains species-specific chromosome number across generations (haploid gametes fuse back to diploid).","Produces genetic variation via crossing over and independent chromosome combination, aiding survival in a changing environment."]
modelAnswer: Two reasons meiosis is useful: (1) Maintenance of chromosome number - diploid germ cells undergo meiosis to produce haploid gametes, so when two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation, the resulting zygote has the normal diploid chromosome number for the species (e.g. humans: 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes), keeping the chromosome number constant across generations. (2) Genetic variation - crossing over and the independent combination of chromosomes during meiosis produce new gene combinations in the gametes, giving offspring genetic variation that helps a species survive in a changing environment.

keyPoints: ["Mitosis: somatic cells, one division, two diploid daughter cells identical to parent","Meiosis: germ cells, two divisions, four haploid daughter cells with new gene combinations"]
modelAnswer: Mitosis and meiosis differ in several ways. Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells, while meiosis occurs in germ line cells. A cell dividing by mitosis divides only once, while a cell undergoing meiosis divides twice. Mitosis produces two daughter cells, while meiosis produces four daughter cells. The daughter cells produced by mitosis are diploid and genetically identical to the parent cell, while all daughter cells produced by meiosis are haploid, with a chromosome number reduced to half that of the parent and a changed genetic makeup due to crossing over. Daughter cells from mitosis become part of the somatic body, while those from meiosis become gametes involved in sexual reproduction.

keyPoints: ["Each organ (two or more tissues together) performs only one specific task.","A full body function usually needs several such specific tasks working together.","An organ system groups organs with related functions so their combined, coordinated action achieves what no single organ could do alone."]
modelAnswer: A single organ, on its own, is made of two or more tissues organised to do just one specific task, for example the heart pumps blood, the lungs bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and the stomach digests food. But no single organ can carry out an entire complex body function by itself. An organ system is a group of organs with related functions that work together to accomplish a larger task that no one organ could do alone, for example the digestive system needs the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver and intestines all cooperating to process food and absorb nutrients. So multiple organs are needed to build an organ system because each organ contributes a specific, specialised part of the overall function, and combining these specialised contributions is what lets the system carry out its complete, coordinated task.

keyPoints: ["DNA is double-stranded, ladder-like, coiled into a helix; strands are antiparallel.","Sugar-phosphate backbone forms the uprights; nitrogenous bases form the rungs.","Chargaff-style rule: adenine = thymine, cytosine = guanine in amount.","Specific complementary base pairing: A-T, C-G, via hydrogen bonds (2 between A-T, 3 between C-G).","Uniform diameter of about 2 nm."]
modelAnswer: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA. Its main points are: (1) DNA is double-stranded, like a ladder, with both strands coiled around each other in a helix. (2) The two strands run antiparallel, meaning they are oriented in opposite directions to each other. (3) The backbone (the uprights of the ladder) of each strand is made of alternating sugar and phosphate groups, while the nitrogenous bases form the rungs of the ladder. (4) The amount of adenine always equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of cytosine always equals the amount of guanine. (5) Base pairing between the two strands is highly specific: adenine on one strand always pairs with thymine on the other, and cytosine always pairs with guanine; because of this rule, the base sequence of one strand is complementary to the sequence of the other. (6) The two strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds: two hydrogen bonds form between adenine and thymine, and three form between cytosine and guanine. (7) The double helix has a uniform diameter of about 2 nanometres throughout its length.

modelAnswer: DNA and RNA differ in at least six features. Strandedness: DNA is double-stranded (two strands coiled as a helix); RNA is single-stranded. Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose sugar; RNA contains ribose sugar. Bases: DNA uses thymine as one of its four bases; RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. Base overhangs: in RNA the nitrogen bases are overhung because they are not bonded to a complementary strand, unlike in DNA where every base is paired. Location/role: DNA is found in the nucleus (in chromosomes) and stores and passes on genetic information; RNA is synthesised in the nucleus but moves to the cytoplasm, acting as an intermediate that carries out protein synthesis. Formation: RNA is synthesised from a DNA template by copying (transcribing) the sequence of one DNA strand.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biologically active globular proteins made by living cells, which tremendously speed up biochemical reactions; they act as biological catalysts. Characteristics of enzymes: (1) each cell synthesises its own enzymes, and which enzymes a cell produces is determined by the genes active in that cell; (2) enzymes act on specific molecules called substrates, converting them into products, and each enzyme is generally specific for its substrate; (3) an enzyme lowers the activation energy needed for a reaction to proceed, without itself being used up or changed permanently; (4) enzymes possess an active site, a three-dimensional region where the substrate binds and reacts; (5) most enzymes need a non-protein cofactor (an inorganic activator, a permanently attached prosthetic group, or a detachable organic coenzyme) to function properly; (6) enzymes work best at a specific optimum temperature and optimum pH, and their activity falls off away from these optimum conditions; (7) enzymes can be located inside the cell (intracellular) or released to work outside the cell (extracellular).

modelAnswer: Both activators and coenzymes are types of cofactors, non-protein components enzymes need to function, but they differ in composition. An activator is a detachable inorganic ion cofactor, for example Zn2+, Fe2+, Cu2+ or chloride ions; for instance, chloride ions increase the activity of salivary amylase. A coenzyme is a detachable organic molecule cofactor, for example NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), coenzyme A, and vitamin A and C. So the key difference is that activators are inorganic ions while coenzymes are organic molecules, though both act as detachable cofactors that assist enzyme activity.

keyPoints: ["Reaction rate rises with temperature up to the enzyme's optimum temperature (about 36-38 C for human enzymes).","Beyond the optimum, the enzyme denatures (active site/shape damaged by vigorous vibration), so rate falls sharply.","At very low temperature the enzyme is inactive but not denatured, just low-energy.","Graph shape: rises, peaks at optimum, then drops sharply."]
modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction increases, but only up to a specific limit. Each enzyme has an optimum temperature at which it works best (for human enzymes this is about 36 to 38 degrees Celsius); different enzymes have different optimum temperatures. Beyond the optimum, further increases in temperature start to damage the enzyme: the atoms of the enzyme molecule vibrate more vigorously, which distorts the enzyme's globular structure and its active site, a process called denaturation, after which the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate effectively and the reaction rate falls sharply. At very low temperatures, the enzyme remains largely inactive (not denatured, just slowed) because low temperature reduces the kinetic energy available for the reaction. (Graph: the reaction-rate curve rises steadily with temperature, peaks sharply at the enzyme's optimum temperature, then drops sharply as temperature rises further past the optimum due to denaturation.)

keyPoints: ["Inhibitor resembles the substrate in shape/structure and occupies the active site.","Blocks the real substrate from binding, so the reaction stops.","Reversible: increasing substrate concentration above inhibitor concentration restores enzyme activity."]
modelAnswer: Competitive inhibition happens when an inhibitor molecule is similar enough in structure and shape to the actual substrate that it can occupy the enzyme's active site in the substrate's place. This inhibitor is not converted into a product, and while it occupies the active site it also prevents the real substrate from binding, so the reaction cannot proceed. Competitive inhibition is temporary and reversible: if the concentration of the actual substrate is raised above the concentration of the inhibitor, the substrate can out-compete the inhibitor for the active site and normal enzyme activity resumes.

keyPoints: ["Inhibitor does not resemble the substrate and does not bind the active site.","It binds a different location on the enzyme, the allosteric site.","This changes the enzyme's overall shape, damaging the active site so the substrate can no longer bind, stopping the reaction."]
modelAnswer: In non-competitive inhibition, the inhibitor molecule's structure and shape do not resemble the substrate, so it does not occupy the enzyme's active site. Instead, it attaches to a different point on the enzyme's surface called the allosteric site. Binding at this site alters the globular shape of the enzyme and damages its active site, so the actual substrate can no longer bind properly, and the reaction stops even though the active site itself was never directly blocked.

topicTitle: 7.6 Role of ATP - the Energy Currency of Cell
keyPoints: ["ATP is an energy-rich compound that stores and releases energy on demand, like money.","Energy released from breaking down glucose/other molecules is captured and stored in ATP.","Hydrolysis of ATP (to ADP + phosphate) releases energy for cell processes (muscle work, active transport, growth, nerve impulses).","ADP is recharged back to ATP by condensation, giving a reusable ATP-ADP cycle."]
modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is called the energy currency of the cell because, like money, it can store and release energy for use whenever and wherever a cell needs it. When organic molecules such as glucose or amino acids are broken down in catabolic reactions, the energy released is captured and stored in ATP molecules until it is needed. When the cell requires energy for processes such as muscle contraction, active transport, growth and repair, or nerve impulse transmission, ATP is hydrolysed (its third phosphate group is removed, converting it to ADP and inorganic phosphate) to release that stored energy. ADP can then be converted back to ATP by condensation, re-storing energy, which is why the ATP-ADP cycle can keep supplying and re-supplying usable energy throughout the cell, exactly as currency is spent and earned again.

keyPoints: ["Aerobic respiration: complete breakdown of glucose using oxygen, releasing a large amount of energy plus CO2 and water.","Step 1, Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose to 2 pyruvic acid, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH.","Step 2, Acetyl CoA formation: pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA, releases CO2, produces NADH.","Step 3, Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix): produces CO2, NADH, FADH2, some ATP.","Step 4, Electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane): NADH/FADH2 electrons generate ATP; oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water."]
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is respiration that takes place in the presence of, and using, oxygen; glucose is completely broken down to release a comparatively large amount of energy, producing carbon dioxide and water as by-products. It occurs in four main phases. (1) Glycolysis: takes place in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration; one glucose molecule is broken down into two 3-carbon pyruvic acid molecules, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. (2) Formation of acetyl CoA: each pyruvic acid molecule is oxidised to a 2-carbon acetyl group, releasing carbon dioxide and producing NADH; the acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA, which enters the mitochondrion. (3) Krebs cycle: takes place in the mitochondrial matrix; coenzyme A is released and the acetyl group passes through a cyclic series of reactions producing CO2, NADH and FADH2, with some ATP made directly. (4) Electron transport chain (ETC): located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, it uses the electrons carried by NADH and FADH2 (each NADH yields about 3 ATP, each FADH2 about 2 ATP); the final electron acceptor is oxygen, which combines with hydrogen ions to form water.

modelAnswer: Three points of comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration: (1) Oxygen requirement - aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen, while anaerobic respiration takes place in its absence. (2) Completeness of breakdown and products - in aerobic respiration glucose is completely broken down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy; in anaerobic respiration glucose is only partially broken down into carbon dioxide and alcohol, or into lactic acid (this is why anaerobic respiration is also called fermentation), releasing much less energy. (3) Energy yield - aerobic respiration yields a comparatively large amount of energy (many ATP molecules, since it uses the full four-phase pathway of glycolysis, acetyl CoA formation, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain), whereas anaerobic respiration, using only glycolysis followed by fermentation, yields far fewer ATP molecules (a net of 2 ATP from glycolysis).

Active absorption spends cellular energy: root cells use respiration-powered transport to take up specific mineral ions against their gradients, drawing water after them osmotically, which is why poisons that stop respiration also stop ion uptake.

keyPoints: ["Stomata are adjustable valves","Ground the answer in the quoted textbook line"]
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the escape of water vapour from aerial plant parts, about ninety percent of it through stomata. It ties directly to cell surface: more leaf area and open stomatal pores mean larger wet surfaces exposed for evaporation. Guard cells regulate this trade-off, swelling to open pores when water is plentiful and collapsing them shut during drought or darkness, so stomatal opening and closing act as the throttle of water loss.

keyPoints: ["Wind strips humidity, heat supplies it","Ground the answer in the quoted textbook line"]
modelAnswer: Temperature raises transpiration by speeding evaporation from mesophyll surfaces, so warmer air means faster water loss, measurable with a potometer's racing bubble. Wind sweeps saturated air away from stomata, steepening the drying gradient and increasing loss. Humidity works oppositely: damp air slows evaporation because the atmosphere already carries nearly all the vapour it can hold.

keyPoints: ["Pushed by pressure, steered by loading","Ground the answer in the quoted textbook line"]
modelAnswer: Pressure-flow explains translocation in steps: companion cells actively load sucrose into sieve tubes at a source, raising solute concentration there; water enters by osmosis, building turgor pressure; at a sink, sugars leave the tube, pressure drops; and the pressure difference pushes sap bodily along the phloem between the two points, delivering food wherever it flows. Loading and unloading control both direction and rate.

keyPoints: ["Transpiration occurs mostly through stomata, found on the leaf surface.","Larger leaf surface area means more stomata, giving a higher transpiration rate.","Smaller/narrower leaf surface area means fewer stomata and lower transpiration rate."]
modelAnswer: Transpiration mainly occurs through the stomata, which are present on the leaf surface, so leaf surface area and transpiration rate are directly related. Plants with a large leaf surface area have more stomata and therefore show a greater rate of transpiration, while plants with narrow, reduced leaf surfaces have fewer stomata and show a lower rate of transpiration.

keyPoints: ["Stomatal transpiration: ~90% of water loss, through leaf/aerial-part stomata.","Cuticular transpiration: ~7-9% of water loss, through the waxy cuticle on the body surface.","Lenticular transpiration: less than 3% of water loss, through lenticels in the stem."]
modelAnswer: There are three types of transpiration. Stomatal transpiration: about 90% of water loss occurs through the stomata, mainly found on the leaves and other aerial parts of the plant. Cuticular transpiration: about 7 to 9% of absorbed water is lost from the general body surface through the waxy cuticle. Lenticular transpiration: a very small amount, less than 3%, is lost through lenticels, which are scar-like regions of ruptured epidermis with loosely packed cortical cells present in the stem.

keyPoints: ["Necessary: cools the plant and drives upward absorption/transport of water and minerals; plants cannot survive without it.","Evil: represents a large, largely unavoidable loss of absorbed water.","Unchecked excessive transpiration can cause wilting and even plant death."]
modelAnswer: Transpiration is called a 'necessary evil' because it is essential for a plant's survival, yet also carries a real cost. It is necessary because it cools the plant and helps absorb water and dissolved minerals, pulling them upward through the plant to the leaves; without transpiration, plants would be unable to survive. It is an 'evil' because it also represents a large, largely unavoidable loss of absorbed water; if this loss becomes excessive and unchecked, it can cause wilting (loss of turgor) and ultimately the death of the plant. So transpiration is both indispensable and potentially harmful at the same time.
stem: Why is transpiration called necessary evil for plants?

keyPoints: ["Transpiration = loss of absorbed water as vapour from the plant's aerial parts, mainly via stomata (~90%).","Larger leaf surface area -> more stomata -> higher transpiration rate.","Stomatal opening/closing directly controls transpiration rate; day (open) > night (closed)."]
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the process by which water absorbed by the roots and moved into the aerial parts of the plant is lost as water vapour into the atmosphere; roughly 99% of absorbed water is eventually lost this way. About 90% of this loss occurs through the stomata, tiny pores mainly present on the leaves and other aerial parts, which is why it is called stomatal transpiration. Role of surface area: leaves with a larger surface area carry more stomata and so show a greater rate of transpiration, while leaves with narrow, reduced surfaces (having fewer stomata) show a lower rate. Role of stomata: since most water loss happens specifically through the stomata, their number and their state of opening or closing directly control the rate of transpiration; more open stomata mean a higher rate of water loss, which is why transpiration is generally greater during the day, when stomata are widely open, than at night, when they are nearly closed.

keyPoints: ["Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed to drive photosynthesis","Light energy plus CO2 and water are used to make glucose","Limiting factors: light intensity and CO2 concentration (also temperature)"]
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll and light are both necessary for photosynthesis because during this process plants absorb light energy in the presence of chlorophyll, and use that energy along with carbon dioxide and water to make glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Without chlorophyll there is no pigment to capture light energy, and without light there is no energy source to drive the reaction. Two factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis are light intensity (more light intensity and duration increases photosynthesis up to a point) and carbon dioxide concentration (CO2 is a raw material for photosynthesis, so more CO2 increases the rate only up to a specific point, beyond which it no longer helps).

keyPoints: ["Sugars actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source (via companion cells), raising solute concentration there.","Water enters the phloem by osmosis at the source, raising pressure (turgor) there.","High pressure at source pushes sap in bulk flow toward the sink (lower pressure).","Sugars unloaded at sink; water leaves the phloem there, lowering pressure and maintaining the pressure gradient."]
modelAnswer: The most widely accepted explanation of how organic solutes (mainly sugars) move through the phloem is the pressure flow (mass flow) theory. Phloem sap contains about 10 to 25 percent dry matter, most of which is sucrose along with some other organic compounds. The mechanism works as follows: sugars produced in source regions (such as photosynthesising leaves or storage organs) are actively loaded into the phloem's sieve tube elements with the help of companion cells. This active loading raises the sugar concentration and lowers the water concentration inside the phloem at the source, making the sieve tube contents more concentrated ('sweeter'). Because of this concentration difference, water moves into the phloem by osmosis from the neighbouring xylem, raising the hydrostatic (turgor) pressure inside the sieve tubes at the source end. This high pressure at the source pushes the phloem sap in bulk (mass flow) through the sieve tubes towards regions of lower pressure, the sink regions (such as roots, fruits or growing tissues) where sugars are being used or stored. At the sink, sugars are unloaded out of the phloem, which raises the water potential inside the sieve tubes there and causes water to move back out into the xylem, lowering the pressure at the sink end. This pressure difference, high at the source and low at the sink, is what drives the continuous mass flow of phloem sap from source to sink. modelAnswer: Osmotic adjustment is the plant's balancing of water against dissolved solutes so cells stay firm without bursting or wilting. In watery habitats hydrophytes keep cell-sap strength near the surroundings and let surplus water exit; in salty or dry spots plants raise cell-sap solutes, holding water against the stronger outside pull; and stomata plus succulent storage tissues fine-tune the daily balance. Osmoregulation thus guards turgor, the quiet force behind every upright stem.

keyPoints: ["Gas waste: CO2 released at night (respiration), O2 released in the day (photosynthesis).","Water waste: excreted continuously through transpiration.","Leaves: store waste/pigments, turn yellow, fall as excretophores.","Stem/branches: waste deposited in old, unused xylem (e.g. ebony heartwood).","Roots: some plants release waste compounds into the soil (e.g. conifers)."]
modelAnswer: Plants excrete waste in several ways, unlike animals which mostly excrete through specialised organs. (1) Excretion of carbon dioxide and oxygen: carbon dioxide, the waste product of respiration, is released at night during gas exchange, while oxygen, the waste product of photosynthesis, is released during the day. (2) Excretion of water: water, a waste product of both photosynthesis and respiration, is excreted through the plant body via transpiration. (3) Excretion through leaves: plant cells store waste substances (including pigmented compounds) in large vacuoles; leaves that accumulate such waste turn yellow and eventually fall in autumn, so these leaves themselves act as an excretory organ and are called excretophores. (4) Excretion through stem and branches: some trees deposit waste chemicals, such as dark pigments, into old xylem tissue in the trunk and branches that is no longer used for water transport (e.g. ebony trees producing dark heartwood). (5) Excretion through roots: some plants actively release waste compounds into the soil through their roots, sometimes using them to chemically compete against neighbouring plants (e.g. conifer trees).

keyPoints: ["CO2 excreted at night (respiration waste); O2 excreted during the day (photosynthesis waste).","Water excreted continuously via transpiration.","Leaves store and remove waste/pigments, yellow and fall as excretophores.","Stem/branches store waste in old xylem (e.g. ebony heartwood).","Roots release waste compounds into soil (e.g. conifers, sometimes for chemical competition)."]
modelAnswer: Unlike animals, excretion in plants is a broad term covering the removal of any waste from the plant body, and plants get rid of waste in several distinct ways. (1) Excretion of carbon dioxide and oxygen: carbon dioxide, produced as a waste of respiration, is released at night during gas exchange, while oxygen, a waste product of photosynthesis, is released during the day. (2) Excretion of water: water is produced as a waste of both photosynthesis and respiration (and is also absorbed from the soil), and it is excreted through the plant body during transpiration. (3) Excretion through leaves: plant vacuoles store waste substances, including pigmented compounds; leaves that build up such waste turn yellow and eventually fall in autumn, acting as an excretory organ, which is why such leaves are also called excretophores. (4) Excretion through stem and branches: some trees deposit unusual waste chemicals in old, no-longer-functional xylem in the trunk and branches, for example the very dark heartwood produced by ebony trees. (5) Excretion through roots: some plants actively release waste compounds into the soil through their roots, sometimes using this as a way to chemically compete with neighbouring plants, as conifer trees are known to do.
stem: Describe different ways of excretion in plants.

keyPoints: ["Lowest transpiration rate","Sunken stomata","Stomata open at night","Thickest cuticle","High water storage (succulence)"]
modelAnswer: Xerophytes are plants adapted to extreme dry conditions, and show several osmotic/water-conservation adjustments compared to hydrophytes and mesophytes: (1) they have the lowest transpiration rates; (2) their stomata are sunken (recessed into the leaf) rather than on the surface; (3) they open their stomata at night rather than during the day, reducing water loss under the heat of daytime; (4) they have the thickest leaf cuticle of the three groups, which reduces water loss through the leaf surface; (5) many xerophytes (succulents) have a high water storage capacity, storing ample water in their tissues.

keyPoints: ["Highest transpiration rate among hydrophytes/mesophytes/xerophytes.","Stomata on the upper leaf surface.","Stomata remain open both day and night.","Almost no cuticle on the leaves (water not limiting)."]
modelAnswer: Hydrophytes (plants living in water-rich environments) show the following osmotic adaptations: (1) they have the highest transpiration rate of the three plant groups (hydrophytes, mesophytes, xerophytes); (2) their stomata are placed on the upper leaf surface (unlike mesophytes, which have them on the lower surface, and xerophytes, which have sunken stomata); (3) their stomata stay open both day and night, unlike mesophytes (open mainly during the day) and xerophytes (open at night); (4) their leaves have almost no cuticle, since water is not a limiting factor for them, compared to the thin cuticle of mesophytes and the thick cuticle of xerophytes.

keyPoints: ["Natural vegetative propagation: happens on its own, from the parent's own structures (roots, stems, leaves, runners, bulbs); no human input.","Artificial vegetative propagation: human-directed, using a removed 'vegetative propagule' (e.g. stem cuttings, grafting, tissue culture/micropropagation).","Both give genetically identical offspring to the parent.","Artificial methods (especially tissue culture) are generally better/faster for large-scale rapid propagation than relying on natural methods alone."]
modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation (natural vegetative propagation) is the process by which plants reproduce asexually on their own, using their own natural mechanisms without human intervention; new plants develop directly from vegetative structures of the parent plant such as roots, stems, leaves, runners, or bulbs, and because they come from the same parent, they carry identical genetic characteristics. Artificial vegetative propagation, by contrast, is used when people purposely propagate plants to meet specific needs (such as preserving good qualities like taste, colour, or disease resistance); it relies on a deliberately removed part of the plant, called a vegetative propagule, using methods such as stem cuttings and grafting that humans carry out rather than the plant achieving on its own. Which is better for rapid propagation: artificial vegetative propagation is generally better for rapid, large-scale propagation, because methods such as stem cuttings, grafting, and especially tissue culture (micropropagation) let growers deliberately and quickly produce large numbers of genetically identical plants under controlled conditions, whereas natural vegetative propagation depends on the plant's own slower, structure-by-structure growth (such as suckers or bulbs forming over time).

modelAnswer: Plant tissue culture (cloning/micropropagation) procedure: (1) A single cell or small piece of tissue is taken from the parent plant; this starting piece is called the explant. (2) The explant is placed on an artificial nutrient medium under aseptic (microbe-free) conditions. (3) The explant's cells divide repeatedly to form an undifferentiated mass of cells called a callus. (4) The callus is treated with plant growth substances to make it first produce shoots, then roots, giving a young plantlet. (5) The plantlets are carefully transferred into soil in natural conditions to continue growing into full plants, each genetically identical to the parent.

modelAnswer: Binary fission (bacteria): a copy of the bacterium's DNA is made so there are two identical sets, which move to opposite ends of the cell. The middle of the cell folds inward, dividing the contents into two, and a new cell wall forms between them, producing two identical daughter bacteria. Budding (yeast): a small outgrowth (bud) forms on one side of the parent yeast cell. The nucleus divides by mitosis into two, and one nucleus moves into the bud. The bud enlarges and comes to resemble the parent; it may then detach as a separate individual, or in some cases stay attached, forming a small connected group of cells.

modelAnswer: Two methods of artificial vegetative propagation: (1) Stem cuttings: a small segment of stem with at least one node is placed in water or damp soil; roots grow from the buried end while the top continues growing leaves. If growth does not start, the cut end is treated with the plant hormone auxin to stimulate rooting; this method is used for roses, ivy, grapevines and chrysanthemums. (2) Grafting: two plant parts are joined to make one new plant. The scion (upper part, carrying the desired fruit/flower traits) is cut and attached to the rootstock (lower part, providing roots and stem support), usually at matching angled cuts, and bound (e.g. with grafting tape) until the graft heals; used for fruit trees and ornamental plants.
stem: Describe any two methods of artificial vegetative propagation in plants.

modelAnswer: Natural vegetative propagation happens without human help, using the plant's own structures: (1) Bulbs: thickened underground stems wrapped in fleshy leaves; shoots from the top and roots from the base grow into new plants (onion, tulip). (2) Corms: thickened underground stems without fleshy leaves; buds at the top give rise to shoots (garlic, dasheen). (3) Rhizomes: horizontal underground stems with nodes; buds on top grow shoots, the underside grows roots (ginger). (4) Stem tubers: swollen underground stem tips with bud 'eyes' that sprout new shoots (potato). (5) Stolons/runners: horizontal stems that grow along the ground from the parent; each node can root and shoot into a new plant (strawberry). (6) Suckers: shoots arising from underground roots or the stem base that become independent plants (lawn grass). (7) Leaves: in Bryophyllum, plantlets form along leaf edges and grow into new plants after falling to the soil.

keyPoints: ["One sperm nucleus + egg cell -> diploid zygote.","Other sperm nucleus + polar nuclei/secondary nucleus -> triploid endosperm nucleus.","Called 'double' because one male gametophyte's two sperm nuclei each carry out a separate fusion; unique to angiosperms."]
modelAnswer: When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, the male gametophyte releases two sperm nuclei. One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, while the other sperm nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei (or secondary nucleus) to form a triploid endosperm nucleus, which develops into the nutritive endosperm tissue. Because one male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei that each carry out a separate fusion in this way, the event is called double fertilization, a feature unique to flowering plants (angiosperms).

keyPoints: ["Pollen grain (microspore) germinates on the stigma after pollination.","Microspore nucleus divides by mitosis into a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus.","Generative nucleus divides again into two sperm nuclei.","Tube nucleus directs pollen-tube growth through the style into the ovule.","Male gametophyte = microspore body + pollen tube + tube nucleus + two sperm nuclei."]
modelAnswer: A flowering plant's life cycle alternates between a diploid sporophyte generation and a haploid gametophyte generation. On the sporophyte, pollen grains (microspores) form in the anther; after pollination, a microspore germinates on the stigma surface to begin forming the male gametophyte. The microspore nucleus first divides by mitosis to form two nuclei: a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus. The generative nucleus divides again to produce two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus controls the growth of the pollen tube, which the microspore forms as it grows down through the style and eventually penetrates the ovule. The complete structure made up of the microspore body, the pollen tube, the tube nucleus, and the two sperm nuclei together is called the male gametophyte. keyPoints: ["Functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis 3 times -> 8 nuclei.","3 nuclei at one end: egg cell (centre) + 2 synergids.","3 nuclei at the other end: antipodals.","2 remaining nuclei in the centre: polar nuclei (may fuse into a secondary nucleus).","Female gametophyte (embryo sac) = megaspore body + 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + polar nuclei + egg."]
modelAnswer: In the flowering-plant life cycle, the female gametophyte develops inside the ovule. The nucleus of the functional megaspore, located in the centre of the ovule, divides three times by mitosis to produce 8 nuclei. Of these, three nuclei migrate to one end of the ovule: the central one becomes the egg cell, and the two beside it become the synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the opposite end and become the antipodals. The two remaining nuclei stay in the centre of the ovule and are called the polar nuclei; in some cases these two fuse together into a single diploid secondary nucleus before the sperm arrives. The complete structure, made up of the megaspore body, the three antipodals, the two synergids, the polar nuclei (or fused secondary nucleus), and the egg cell, together is called the female gametophyte, or embryo sac. (Sketch: draw the ovule containing the embryo sac with the egg cell and two synergids at the micropylar end, the two polar nuclei in the centre, and the three antipodal cells at the opposite (chalazal) end.)

modelAnswer: When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, one of its two sperm nuclei fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, and the other sperm nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei (or the fused secondary nucleus) to form a triploid endosperm nucleus. Because a single male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei that each fuse with a different nucleus in the embryo sac, this event is called double fertilization. It is unique to flowering plants (angiosperms) and produces both the zygote (which becomes the embryo) and the endosperm nucleus (which becomes the nutritive endosperm tissue of the seed).

modelAnswer: The embryo sac is the female gametophyte of a flowering plant, formed inside the ovule. The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides three times by mitosis to produce 8 nuclei. Three of these migrate to one end of the ovule: the central one becomes the egg cell, flanked by two synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the opposite end and become the antipodals. The remaining two nuclei move to the centre of the ovule as polar nuclei, which may fuse into a single diploid secondary nucleus before fertilization. So the embryo sac consists of 1 egg cell, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, and 2 polar nuclei (or 1 secondary nucleus), 8 nuclei in total.

modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction is more beneficial than asexual reproduction because it involves the fusion of gametes from two different parents, which mixes and shuffles genetic material through meiosis. This produces offspring that are genetically varied rather than exact clones. Cross pollination, in particular, ensures more genetic variability in successive generations. This variability gives a population a greater range of traits to draw on, improving its ability to adapt and survive changing conditions, which asexual reproduction (offspring genetically identical to a single parent) cannot provide.

modelAnswer: Male gametophyte: after pollination, a pollen grain (microspore) germinates on the stigma. Its nucleus divides by mitosis into a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus; the generative nucleus divides again to form two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus directs growth of the pollen tube down through the style into the ovule. The whole structure (microspore body, pollen tube, tube nucleus, and two sperm nuclei) is the male gametophyte. Female gametophyte (embryo sac): the functional megaspore's nucleus inside the ovule divides three times by mitosis to give 8 nuclei. Three migrate to one end (the central one becomes the egg, flanked by two synergids); three migrate to the other end (the antipodals); the remaining two become polar nuclei at the centre, which may fuse into a diploid secondary nucleus. This whole structure (egg, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, 2 polar nuclei/secondary nucleus) is the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

modelAnswer: Seed germination is the process by which a seed absorbs water, swells, breaks its seed coat, and grows into a seedling, marking the start of a new plant's life. There are two types: (1) Epigeal germination, where the hypocotyl elongates and forms a hook that pulls the cotyledons above the ground (e.g. beans, cotton, papaya). (2) Hypogeal germination, where the epicotyl elongates and forms the hook while the cotyledons stay underground (e.g. peas, maize, coconut). Conditions needed for germination: internally, the seed must contain a living embryo and enough stored food; externally, it needs water (moisture, to soak the seed and mobilize stored food), oxygen (for the embryo's cells to respire), and a suitable temperature (about 25-30°C for most plants).

modelAnswer: A typical flower consists of a stalk (pedicel) that holds it up, topped by a swollen platform called the thalamus. The thalamus bears four whorls of floral leaves. The outermost whorl is the calyx, made of green sepals that protect the inner parts. Just inside is the corolla, made of coloured petals. The calyx and corolla take no direct part in reproduction, so together they are called the accessory whorls. Inside the corolla is the androecium (the male whorl), made of stamens that produce pollen; each stamen has a filament and an anther containing pollen sacs. At the centre is the gynoecium (the female whorl), made of one or more carpels/pistils, each with an ovary (containing ovules), a style, and a stigma. The androecium and gynoecium actually carry out reproduction, so they are called the necessary whorls.

modelAnswer: The key points of Darwin's theory of natural selection are: (1) Overproduction - all living creatures are highly fertile, so their populations could grow quickly and produce large numbers of offspring. (2) Competition - because food supplies and other resources are limited, population sizes stay largely constant despite overproduction, creating competition for resources. (3) Variation - no two organisms are the same; individuals differ, they do not have equal chances of survival and reproduction, and much of this variation is heritable, passed on to offspring through genes. (4) Natural selection - only organisms that survive and reproduce give rise to the next generation, and only those with favourable (advantageous) variations tend to survive to reproductive age; over many generations, the population accumulates more advantageous genetic variations and fewer harmful ones, since natural selection is essentially a process of elimination in which only the fittest survive.

keyPoints: ["Comparative anatomy: evidence via homologous structures and vestigial structures.","Homologous structures: similar structure/arrangement in different species (e.g. limb bones), despite different functions, points to a shared ancestor.","Vestigial structures: reduced, largely non-functional remnants of structures that were useful in an ancestor, showing descent with modification."]
modelAnswer: Comparative anatomy is one of the pieces of evidence for evolution, and it works through homologous structures and vestigial structures. Homologous structures are body parts in different species that have a similar underlying structure and arrangement (for example the bones of a bat's wing, a human arm, and a whale's flipper), even though the organisms use them for very different purposes; this similarity is best explained by the different species having descended from a common ancestor and then adapting the same basic structure to different needs over time. Vestigial structures are reduced, seemingly non-functional body parts (structures that were functional in an ancestor) that are still present in a species; their presence is evidence that the species evolved from an ancestor in which the structure had a purpose, and evolution has since reduced its usefulness. Together, these anatomical similarities and leftover structures across species are strong evidence that different organisms share a common evolutionary origin.

keyPoints: ["Palaeontology = study of fossils (the fossil record).","Fossils in rock layers can be ordered chronologically by the age of the layer.","The record shows gradual change in traits over time, including transitional forms.","This gradual, ordered change is evidence that species descended with modification from earlier ancestors."]
modelAnswer: Palaeontology, the study of fossils, provides evidence for evolution through the fossil record. Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of organisms that lived in the past, and when they are found in successive layers of rock they can be arranged in the chronological order in which the rock layers were laid down. This ordered fossil record shows a gradual change in the traits of related organisms over long spans of time, with older rock layers generally containing simpler or more primitive forms and younger layers showing forms progressively more similar to species alive today, including transitional fossils that share features of two different groups. This gradual, layered pattern of change captured in the fossil record is strong evidence that today's species descended, with modification, from earlier ancestral forms, which is the central claim of evolution.

Remove and dry the paper before the solvent reaches the top, then measure distances travelled by spots and solvent front to calculate Rf values.

modelAnswer: Computer generations are grouped by their major technological developments. First-generation computers used vacuum tubes. They were large, consumed considerable power, generated heat, and were less reliable. In the second generation, transistors replaced vacuum tubes, making computers smaller, faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective; programming also advanced to assembly and high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL. Third-generation computers used integrated circuits, which placed multiple transistors on a single chip and further improved size, speed, and efficiency. Fourth-generation computers introduced microprocessors, integrating the processing unit onto a single chip using large-scale and very-large-scale integration. This led to much smaller and more capable personal computers. Fifth-generation computers focus on artificial intelligence and natural-language processing. They are intended to learn, reason, and solve problems autonomously. Each generation therefore increased processing capability while reducing size, cost, and power requirements.

modelAnswer: Natural and artificial systems are collections of connected parts that work together, but they differ in origin. Natural systems occur organically without human design. They are often self-regulating, adaptable, and stable. Examples include an ecosystem such as a forest or aquatic environment, weather patterns, the solar system, and the human body. Their parts interact according to natural processes and laws. Artificial systems are designed and built by people to meet a need or solve a problem. They may require maintenance and operate according to planned rules. Examples include communication networks such as telephone and Internet systems, databases and software, transport systems, power plants, manufacturing robots, and medical devices. Studying both kinds of systems is important because it helps us understand how interconnected parts, inputs, processes, and outputs work together. It also helps engineers and scientists design, manage, and improve artificial systems while learning from the efficiency and adaptability found in nature.

modelAnswer: The five fundamental components of network communication are sender, message, medium, receiver, and protocol. The sender, also called the transmitter, is the device that sends the information. It converts the electrical signal into a form suitable for transmission. The message is the data being sent, such as text, audio, or video. The medium is the path through which the message travels, for example a telephone cable, fibre optic cable, Wi-Fi, or a radio wave. The receiver is the destination device, such as a computer, telephone, or television, that accepts the transmitted message and converts it to an appropriate form. A protocol is the agreed set of rules that governs the communication and allows the devices to understand one another. During a transfer, the sender encodes the message, the medium carries it, and the receiver decodes it according to the protocol. Together these components allow data to move reliably from its source to its destination.

keyPoints: ["A hub broadcasts data to every connected device with no intelligence.","A switch forwards data only to the intended destination device, improving efficiency.","A router directs data between different networks, choosing the best path.","A gateway connects networks that use different protocols, translating between them so devices on each can communicate."]
modelAnswer: A hub connects several devices in a local area network and broadcasts incoming data to every connected device. It is simple but inefficient because devices receive data not intended for them. A switch is more intelligent: it examines the packet, identifies the intended device, and sends the packet only there, reducing traffic and improving efficiency. A router connects different networks, often a local network to the Internet. It selects an appropriate path for packets and forwards them between networks. A gateway connects networks that use different protocols. It translates data formats so the networks can communicate, such as a PC network communicating with an IBM mainframe network. In practice, a hub is suitable only for a basic small network, a switch is preferred for efficient communication inside a LAN, a router is needed for communication between networks, and a gateway is used where protocol conversion is required.

keyPoints: ["Bus topology: simple and cheap to install, but a single cable failure can bring down the whole network; suits small, temporary networks.","Star topology: each device connects to a central hub/switch, easy to manage and a single device failure does not affect others, but the whole network fails if the central device fails; suits most modern office/home networks.","Ring topology: data travels in one direction around a ring, predictable performance, but one broken link can disrupt the whole ring unless dual-ring redundancy is used; suits networks needing orderly, predictable data flow."]
modelAnswer: A bus topology connects all devices to one central cable. It is simple and cost-effective for small networks, but a damaged bus cable can affect the entire network. A star topology connects every device to a central hub or switch. It is easy to maintain and expand, and an individual cable failure normally affects only one device, but failure of the central hub or switch brings down the network. A ring topology connects devices in a circular arrangement and sends data around the loop in one direction. It can be cost-effective and provides an orderly path, but a break anywhere in the ring can stop the whole network. A small temporary network with limited cost may use bus. A school or office LAN normally benefits from star because it is easier to troubleshoot and extend. Ring is suitable where controlled one-way circulation is useful and the organisation can tolerate or protect against the effect of a break.

keyPoints: ["The OSI model is a 7-layer conceptual framework describing how data moves from one device to another across a network.","Physical: transmits raw bits over the medium. Data Link: handles node-to-node delivery and error detection. Network: routes data between different networks. Transport: ensures reliable end-to-end delivery.","Session: manages and controls the dialogue/session between devices. Presentation: converts data into a standard format (e.g. encryption, compression). Application: provides the interface for end-user software to access network services.","Breaking communication into these layers helps engineers design, troubleshoot and standardize network technology independently at each layer."]
modelAnswer: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a conceptual framework that explains how networking protocols cooperate to transmit data. It has seven layers. The Application layer provides end-user services such as file transfer and reading messages. The Presentation layer converts data into a format understood by other layers and systems. The Session layer establishes and manages communication sessions between applications. The Transport layer provides reliable delivery and maintains packet order and integrity. The Network layer chooses an efficient path for data and uses devices such as routers. The Data Link layer defines the data format for the link, converts data into packets or frames, and checks accuracy. The Physical layer transmits the actual bits through physical hardware such as cables and connectors. Data moves down the layers at the sender, crosses the medium, and moves up the layers at the receiver. Separating the work into layers makes network design, compatibility, troubleshooting, and protocol development easier to understand.

modelAnswer: A traditional algorithm follows an explicitly designed sequence of rules or a formula, so its operations can usually be inspected and reproduced. $\frac{\sec\theta+1}{\sec\theta-1}$.
ix. Shown in v: $\sec^{2}\theta+\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\cos^{2}}=\sec^{2}\theta\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta$.
x. With $a=\sin^{2}, b=\cos^{2}$: $a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)^{3}-3ab(a+b)=1-3\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$.

modelAnswer:
The errors are in array creation and loop bounds:

1. (a) uses parentheses: `const myArray = ("apple", 3.14, true, "orange");` It must use square brackets `[]`.
2. (b) has no brackets: `const myArray = "apple", 3.14, true, "orange";` It must be `["apple", 3.14, true, "orange"]`.
3. (c) uses `for (i = 0; i <= numbers.length; i ++)` with undeclared `i` and `<=` which reads one past the end. Use `for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++)`.
4. (d) uses `for (i = numbers.length; i < 0; i--)` which never runs. Use `for (let i = numbers.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)` or forward loop from 0.

keyPoints: ["Dividing the volume polynomial by the given height factors out the remaining quadratic, which itself factors into the other two box dimensions."]
modelAnswer:
Volume $=x^3+2x^2-5x-6$, height $=x-2$. Dividing the volume by the height (synthetic division by root 2 on coefficients $1,2,-5,-6$): quotient $=x^2+4x+3=(x+1)(x+3)$, remainder 0.

So Volume $=(x-2)(x+1)(x+3)$. Since height $=x-2$, the remaining factor $(x+1)(x+3)$ gives length and width: length $=x+3$, width $=x+1$ (the two linear dimensions multiplying with height to give the volume).

keyPoints: ["Solution, root, and zero of a function all describe the same idea (a value making the equation/function equal zero); the x-intercept is that value's location on the graph."]
modelAnswer:
i. **Solution**: a value of the variable that satisfies (makes true) the equation.

ii. **Root**: a value of $x$ for which a polynomial equation equals zero; for a quadratic $ax^2+bx+c=0$ the roots are the values of $x$ satisfying it.

iii. **Zero of a function**: a value of $x$ for which $f(x)=0$; identical in meaning to a root when the function is set equal to zero.

iv. **x-intercept**: the point(s) where the graph of $y=f(x)$ crosses the x-axis, i.e. where $y=0$ -- its x-coordinate is exactly a root/zero of the function.

keyPoints: ["A degree-2 polynomial equation has at most 2 roots -- this bound comes directly from factoring into at most two linear factors."]
modelAnswer: No. A quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ can have at most two solutions. Factoring the left side always gives (at most) two linear factors, $a(x-r_1)(x-r_2)=0$, and by the zero product property each factor contributes exactly one root -- so there are exactly two roots (counted with multiplicity: a repeated root when $D=0$ counts as one value appearing twice, and no real root at all when $D<0$, but never more than two). This follows from the equation being degree 2: a polynomial of degree n has at most n roots.

modelAnswer:
Substitution used to reduce each to quadratic form:

i. $ax^4+bx^2+c=0$: let $y=x^2$, giving $ay^2+by+c=0$.

ii. $9x^6-3x^3+7=0$: let $y=x^3$, giving $9y^2-3y+7=0$.

iv. $(x+1)^2+\dfrac{3}{(x+1)^2}=4$: let $y=(x+1)^2$, giving $y+\dfrac{3}{y}=4 \Rightarrow y^2-4y+3=0$.

v. $3\left(x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}\right)+8\left(x+\dfrac1x\right)+11=0$: let $y=x+\dfrac1x$, so $x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}=y^2-2$, giving $3(y^2-2)+8y+11=0 \Rightarrow 3y^2+8y+5=0$.

vi. $3x^4+7x^3+5x^2-7x+3=0$: divide by $x^2$ and let $y=x-\dfrac1x$ (so $x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}=y^2+2$): $3(y^2+2)+7y+5=0 \Rightarrow 3y^2+7y+11=0$.

vii. $ak^{2x}+bk^{x}+c=0$: let $y=k^{x}$, giving $ay^2+by+c=0$.

viii. $8\times4^{x}-7\times2^{x}-1=0$: since $4^x=(2^x)^2$, let $y=2^x$, giving $8y^2-7y-1=0$.

ix. $(x-1)(x-2)(x+3)(x-6)=6$: pairing roots so the linear terms match, $(x-1)(x-2)=x^2-3x+2$ and $(x+3)(x-6)=x^2-3x-18$. Let $y=x^2-3x$: $(y+2)(y-18)=6 \Rightarrow y^2-16y-36=6 \Rightarrow y^2-16y-42=0$.

topicTitle: 2.3 Nature of Roots of a Quadratic Equation
keyPoints: ["Expanding the discriminant reduces it to -4(ad-bc)^2, a negative-or-zero quantity, which is the algebraic reason the roots are imaginary except in the ad=bc boundary case."]
modelAnswer:
$(a^2+b^2)x^2+2(ac+bd)x+(c^2+d^2)=0$: discriminant

$D=[2(ac+bd)]^2-4(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=4\left[(ac+bd)^2-(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)\right]$

Expanding: $(ac+bd)^2=a^2c^2+2abcd+b^2d^2$ and $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=a^2c^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2+b^2d^2$.

Difference $=2abcd-a^2d^2-b^2c^2=-(a^2d^2-2abcd+b^2c^2)=-(ad-bc)^2$.

So $D=-4(ad-bc)^2 \le 0$ always, since $(ad-bc)^2\ge0$. A discriminant $\le0$ means the roots are imaginary (equal only in the boundary case $D=0$). So the roots are imaginary in general, and $D=0$ exactly when $(ad-bc)^2=0$, i.e. $ad=bc$ -- at which point the (equal) roots are real rather than imaginary, matching the claim.

keyPoints: ["A degree-2 polynomial equation has at most 2 roots -- this bound comes directly from factoring into at most two linear factors."]
modelAnswer: No. A quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ can have at most two solutions. Factoring the left side always gives (at most) two linear factors, $a(x-r_1)(x-r_2)=0$, and by the zero product property each factor contributes exactly one root -- so there are exactly two roots (counted with multiplicity: a repeated root when $D=0$ counts as one value appearing twice, and no real root at all when $D<0$, but never more than two). This follows from the equation being degree 2: a polynomial of degree n has at most n roots.

If $b=ac$: $D=16b(b-ac)=16b(0)=0$, so the roots are equal. This confirms the claim: $b=ac$ is sufficient for equal roots (the equation $16b(b-ac)=0$ shows $b=0$ also gives equal roots as a separate case, but $b=ac$ is the condition asked about here).

keyPoints: ["Matrix equality requires identical order and every corresponding entry equal; mismatched orders make equality impossible regardless of variable values."]
modelAnswer:
Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order AND every corresponding entry matches.

(a) $[x\ \ 9]=[2\ \ y]$: $x=2,\ y=9$

(b) $\begin{bmatrix}6&3\\4&x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&3\\4&0\end{bmatrix}$: **not possible** -- the (1,1) entries $6\neq7$ already conflict, regardless of $x$.

(c) $\begin{bmatrix}5x\\2y\end{bmatrix}$ (order $2\times1$) $=[-10\ \ 20]$ (order $1\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ.

(d) $-\begin{bmatrix}2x&3y\\4z&10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}-2x&-3y\\-4z&-10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix}$: the $(2,2)$ entries match ($-10=-10$); $-2x=8\Rightarrow x=-4$; $-3y=6\Rightarrow y=-2$; $-4z=32\Rightarrow z=-8$.

(e) $\begin{bmatrix}x&-2y\\6&x+y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-6\\6&z\end{bmatrix}$: $x=3$; $-2y=-6\Rightarrow y=3$; $x+y=z\Rightarrow z=6$.

(f) $\begin{bmatrix}5\\6\\7\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times1$) $=\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\x&0\\7&0\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ regardless of $x$.

(g) $\begin{bmatrix}x+y\\x-y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}11\\1\end{bmatrix}$: $x+y=11,\ x-y=1 \Rightarrow x=6,\ y=5$.

(h) $\begin{bmatrix}5&10\\15&x\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}5&y\\15&5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}10&10+y\\30&x+5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix}$: $z=10$; $10+y=15\Rightarrow y=5$; $x+5=7\Rightarrow x=2$.

(i) $5\begin{bmatrix}x\\3y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}36\\26\end{bmatrix}=2\begin{bmatrix}-2x\\y\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}5x-36\\15y-26\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4x\\2y\end{bmatrix}$: $5x-36=-4x\Rightarrow x=4$; $15y-26=2y\Rightarrow y=2$.

(j) $\begin{bmatrix}x&y&z\\-2&-4&5\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}5&3&2\\1&6&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&8&11\end{bmatrix}$: second row automatically checks out ($-2+2=0,-4+12=8,5+6=11$). First row: $x+10=0\Rightarrow x=-10$; $y+6=0\Rightarrow y=-6$; $z+4=0\Rightarrow z=-4$.

keyPoints: ["Matrix equality requires identical order and every corresponding entry equal; mismatched orders make equality impossible regardless of variable values."]
modelAnswer:
Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order AND every corresponding entry matches.

(a) $[x\ \ 9]=[2\ \ y]$: $x=2,\ y=9$

(b) $\begin{bmatrix}6&3\\4&x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&3\\4&0\end{bmatrix}$: **not possible** -- the (1,1) entries $6\neq7$ already conflict, regardless of $x$.

(c) $\begin{bmatrix}5x\\2y\end{bmatrix}$ (order $2\times1$) $=[-10\ \ 20]$ (order $1\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ.

(d) $-\begin{bmatrix}2x&3y\\4z&10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}-2x&-3y\\-4z&-10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix}$: the $(2,2)$ entries match ($-10=-10$); $-2x=8\Rightarrow x=-4$; $-3y=6\Rightarrow y=-2$; $-4z=32\Rightarrow z=-8$.

(e) $\begin{bmatrix}x&-2y\\6&x+y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-6\\6&z\end{bmatrix}$: $x=3$; $-2y=-6\Rightarrow y=3$; $x+y=z\Rightarrow z=6$.

(f) $\begin{bmatrix}5\\6\\7\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times1$) $=\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\x&0\\7&0\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ regardless of $x$.

(g) $\begin{bmatrix}x+y\\x-y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}11\\1\end{bmatrix}$: $x+y=11,\ x-y=1 \Rightarrow x=6,\ y=5$.

(h) $\begin{bmatrix}5&10\\15&x\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}5&y\\15&5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}10&10+y\\30&x+5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix}$: $z=10$; $10+y=15\Rightarrow y=5$; $x+5=7\Rightarrow x=2$.

(i) $5\begin{bmatrix}x\\3y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}36\\26\end{bmatrix}=2\begin{bmatrix}-2x\\y\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}5x-36\\15y-26\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4x\\2y\end{bmatrix}$: $5x-36=-4x\Rightarrow x=4$; $15y-26=2y\Rightarrow y=2$.

(j) $\begin{bmatrix}x&y&z\\-2&-4&5\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}5&3&2\\1&6&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&8&11\end{bmatrix}$: second row automatically checks out ($-2+2=0,-4+12=8,5+6=11$). First row: $x+10=0\Rightarrow x=-10$; $y+6=0\Rightarrow y=-6$; $z+4=0\Rightarrow z=-4$.

keyPoints: ["Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general (AB != BA), so identities like (A+B)(A-B) = A^2-B^2 that rely on commutativity fail for matrices even though they hold for numbers.","The transpose-of-a-product rule is (AB)^t = B^t A^t (order reverses)."]
modelAnswer:
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}$, $C=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}$

(i) $AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&-7\end{bmatrix}$, $BA=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\-6&-9\end{bmatrix}$. $AB\neq BA$ (matrix multiplication is not commutative).

(ii) $AC=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, $CA=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$. $AC=CA$ (this particular pair happens to commute).

(iii) $A(B+C)=\begin{bmatrix}5&1\\4&-4\end{bmatrix}$; $AB+AC=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&-7\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5&1\\4&-4\end{bmatrix}$. Verified equal.

(iv) $(A-B)C=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\-6&6\end{bmatrix}$; $AC-BC=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\6&-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\-6&6\end{bmatrix}$. Verified equal.

(v) Associative property: $(AB)C=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\26&-7\end{bmatrix}$ and $A(BC)=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\26&-7\end{bmatrix}$. Equal, so $(AB)C=A(BC)$ is verified.

(vi) $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\8&9\end{bmatrix}$, $B^2=\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\0&9\end{bmatrix}$, $A+B=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&0\end{bmatrix}$, $A-B=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\2&6\end{bmatrix}$, $(A+B)(A-B)=\begin{bmatrix}-1&3\\-2&-2\end{bmatrix}$, $A^2-B^2=\begin{bmatrix}-3&1\\8&0\end{bmatrix}$.

(vii) $(A+B)(A-B)\stackrel?=A^2-B^2$: $\begin{bmatrix}-1&3\\-2&-2\end{bmatrix}\neq\begin{bmatrix}-3&1\\8&0\end{bmatrix}$. **Not equal** -- this algebraic identity requires $AB=BA$, which fails here.

(viii) $(A-B)(A+B)=\begin{bmatrix}-5&-1\\18&2\end{bmatrix}$, also **not equal** to $A^2-B^2$.

(ix) $(A+B)(A-B)\stackrel?=(A-B)(A+B)$: $\begin{bmatrix}-1&3\\-2&-2\end{bmatrix}\neq\begin{bmatrix}-5&-1\\18&2\end{bmatrix}$. **Not equal**, confirming matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

(x) $(AB)^t=\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&-7\end{bmatrix}$; $B^tA^t=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&-3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&-7\end{bmatrix}$. Equal, verifying $(AB)^t=B^tA^t$. Also $(A^t)^t=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{bmatrix}=A$, verified.

keyPoints: ["Matrix Inversion Method and Cramer's rule both require a non-singular coefficient matrix (determinant ≠ 0).","When both given equations reduce to the same line, the determinant is 0 and the system has infinitely many solutions rather than a unique pair."]
modelAnswer:
**(a) Matrix Inversion Method**

(i) $4x+3y=-6,\ x+2y=1$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=8-3=5$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-6\\1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-15\\10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\2\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=-3,\ y=2$.

(ii) $-x+2y=1.5,\ 5x+4y=3$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\5&4\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=-4-10=-14$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.5\\3\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}0\\-10.5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0.75\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=0,\ y=0.75$.

(iii) $2y=10-16x,\ 24x=15-3y$. Rearranged: $16x+2y=10$ (divide by 2: $8x+y=5$) and $24x+3y=15$ (divide by 3: $8x+y=5$). Both reduce to the **same equation**, so the coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $48-48=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; the system has infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

(iv) $9-x=7y,\ 14y+2x=18$. Rearranged: $x+7y=9$ and $2x+14y=18$ (divide by 2: $x+7y=9$). Again the **same equation** twice, so $\begin{bmatrix}-1&-7\\2&14\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-14-(-14)=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; infinitely many solutions along $x+7y=9$.

**(b) Cramer's Rule**

(i) $2x+3y=5,\ 5x+10y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-15=5$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\10&10\end{vmatrix}=50-30=20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}2&5\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-25=-5$. $x=20/5=4,\ y=-5/5=-1$.

(ii) $x=\frac{2}{3}-2y \Rightarrow x+2y=\frac{2}{3}$; $4y=3-3x \Rightarrow 3x+4y=3$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=4-6=-2$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}2/3&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=8/3-6=-10/3$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}1&2/3\\3&3\end{vmatrix}=3-2=1$. $x=\frac{-10/3}{-2}=\frac{5}{3},\ y=\frac{1}{-2}=-\frac{1}{2}$.

(iii) $\frac{6}{10}x+\frac{8}{10}y=20 \Rightarrow 0.6x+0.8y=20$; $\frac{8}{10}x-\frac{6}{10}y=10 \Rightarrow 0.8x-0.6y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&0.8\\0.8&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-0.36-0.64=-1$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}20&0.8\\10&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-12-8=-20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&20\\0.8&10\end{vmatrix}=6-16=-10$. $x=-20/-1=20,\ y=-10/-1=10$.

(iv) $16x-10+2y=0 \Rightarrow 16x+2y=10$; $15-3y-24x=0 \Rightarrow 24x+3y=15$. Dividing gives $8x+y=5$ in both cases: the **same equation**, so $D=\begin{vmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{vmatrix}=48-48=0$. Cramer's rule **fails** (D = 0); infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

$Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$, $Z=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$.

$YZ=\begin{bmatrix}1(2)+2(1)&1(3)+2(2)\\2(2)+3(1)&2(3)+3(2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4&7\\7&12\end{bmatrix}$, $|YZ|=48-49=-1$, $(YZ)^{-1}=\dfrac1{-1}\begin{bmatrix}12&-7\\-7&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-12&7\\7&-4\end{bmatrix}$.

$|Y|=3-4=-1 \Rightarrow Y^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}-3&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}$. $|Z|=4-3=1 \Rightarrow Z^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.

$Z^{-1}Y^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2(-3)+(-3)(2)&2(2)+(-3)(-1)\\-1(-3)+2(2)&-1(2)+2(-1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-12&7\\7&-4\end{bmatrix}$

This equals $(YZ)^{-1}$, verifying $(YZ)^{-1}=Z^{-1}Y^{-1}$.

keyPoints: ["When the coefficient matrix's determinant is 0, the Matrix Inversion Method (and Cramer's rule) cannot produce a unique solution -- check whether the system is dependent (same line, infinite solutions) or inconsistent (parallel lines, no solution)."]
modelAnswer:
Rearranging: $5x-4=y \Rightarrow 5x-y=4$; $2y+8=10x \Rightarrow -10x+2y=-8$.

Matrix form: $\begin{bmatrix}5&-1\\-10&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\-8\end{bmatrix}$.

$|A|=5(2)-(-1)(-10)=10-10=0$: the coefficient matrix is **singular**, so its inverse does not exist and the Matrix Inversion Method cannot be used.

In fact, the second equation $-10x+2y=-8$ simplifies (dividing by $-2$) to $5x-y=4$ -- exactly the first equation. So the system is dependent (both equations describe the same line), giving infinitely many solutions rather than a unique one.

keyPoints: ["A singular coefficient matrix (determinant zero) with proportional equations means the system is dependent, not solvable uniquely.","Check whether one equation is a scalar multiple of the other before assuming a unique matrix solution exists."]
modelAnswer:
Let $l$ = labour cost rate per worker, $m$ = material cost rate per item (same rates for both industries).

Haani's: 6 workers, 80 items, total Rs. 20,000: $6l+80m=20000$.

Massab's: 12 workers, 160 items, total Rs. 40,000: $12l+160m=40000$.

Notice the second equation is exactly **twice** the first ($12=2\times6$, $160=2\times80$, $40000=2\times20000$). The coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}6&80\\12&160\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $6(160)-80(12)=960-960=0$, so it is singular.

The two equations are dependent (the same relationship scaled up), so the labour rate $l$ and material rate $m$ **cannot be uniquely determined** from this data alone; only their combination $6l+80m=20000$ is fixed, with infinitely many $(l,m)$ pairs satisfying it.

Matrix form: $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0.55&0.80\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}20\\14\end{bmatrix}$. $|A|=0.80-0.55=0.25$.

keyPoints: ["Matrix Inversion Method and Cramer's rule both require a non-singular coefficient matrix (determinant ≠ 0).","When both given equations reduce to the same line, the determinant is 0 and the system has infinitely many solutions rather than a unique pair."]
modelAnswer:
**(a) Matrix Inversion Method**

(i) $4x+3y=-6,\ x+2y=1$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=8-3=5$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-6\\1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-15\\10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\2\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=-3,\ y=2$.

(ii) $-x+2y=1.5,\ 5x+4y=3$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\5&4\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=-4-10=-14$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.5\\3\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}0\\-10.5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0.75\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=0,\ y=0.75$.

(iii) $2y=10-16x,\ 24x=15-3y$. Rearranged: $16x+2y=10$ (divide by 2: $8x+y=5$) and $24x+3y=15$ (divide by 3: $8x+y=5$). Both reduce to the **same equation**, so the coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $48-48=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; the system has infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

(iv) $9-x=7y,\ 14y+2x=18$. Rearranged: $x+7y=9$ and $2x+14y=18$ (divide by 2: $x+7y=9$). Again the **same equation** twice, so $\begin{bmatrix}-1&-7\\2&14\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-14-(-14)=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; infinitely many solutions along $x+7y=9$.

**(b) Cramer's Rule**

(i) $2x+3y=5,\ 5x+10y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-15=5$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\10&10\end{vmatrix}=50-30=20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}2&5\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-25=-5$. $x=20/5=4,\ y=-5/5=-1$.

(ii) $x=\frac{2}{3}-2y \Rightarrow x+2y=\frac{2}{3}$; $4y=3-3x \Rightarrow 3x+4y=3$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=4-6=-2$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}2/3&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=8/3-6=-10/3$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}1&2/3\\3&3\end{vmatrix}=3-2=1$. $x=\frac{-10/3}{-2}=\frac{5}{3},\ y=\frac{1}{-2}=-\frac{1}{2}$.

(iii) $\frac{6}{10}x+\frac{8}{10}y=20 \Rightarrow 0.6x+0.8y=20$; $\frac{8}{10}x-\frac{6}{10}y=10 \Rightarrow 0.8x-0.6y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&0.8\\0.8&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-0.36-0.64=-1$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}20&0.8\\10&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-12-8=-20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&20\\0.8&10\end{vmatrix}=6-16=-10$. $x=-20/-1=20,\ y=-10/-1=10$.

(iv) $16x-10+2y=0 \Rightarrow 16x+2y=10$; $15-3y-24x=0 \Rightarrow 24x+3y=15$. Dividing gives $8x+y=5$ in both cases: the **same equation**, so $D=\begin{vmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{vmatrix}=48-48=0$. Cramer's rule **fails** (D = 0); infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

keyPoints: ["A relation is a function from A to B only if its domain is exactly A and no element of A repeats as a first component.","R1 and R4 satisfy both conditions; R2 has a repeated first element (6) and R3 has domain missing 4."]
modelAnswer:
A relation from A to B is a function only if its domain equals A and no element of A repeats as a first component (each maps to exactly one image in B).

i. $R_1=\{(2,3),(6,5),(8,3),(4,1)\}$: domain $=\{2,6,8,4\}=A$, no first-element repeats, all images in B. **Function.**

ii. $R_2=\{(2,3),(6,1),(8,3),(6,5)\}$: 6 appears twice, mapped to both 1 and 5. **Not a function.**

iii. $R_3=\{(2,3),(6,5),(8,3)\}$: domain $=\{2,6,8\}\neq A$ (4 is missing). **Not a function.**

iv. $R_4=\{(2,3),(6,3),(8,3),(4,1)\}$: domain $=\{2,6,8,4\}=A$, no repeats. **Function.**

So $R_1$ and $R_4$ are functions from A to B.

modelAnswer: Let $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{b}$, with $A$ at the origin. Then vertices are $A=0$, $B=\vec{a}$, $D=\vec{b}$, $C=\vec{a}+\vec{b}$. Opposite sides are equal and parallel, so $\overrightarrow{DC} = \overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{b}$, while $\overrightarrow{DA} = -\vec{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD} = -\vec{a}$ by direction. Diagonal $\overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ by triangle law. Diagonal $\overrightarrow{DB} = \overrightarrow{AB} - \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$, and $\overrightarrow{BD} = -\overrightarrow{DB} = -\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. Let $O$ be the intersection of the diagonals, so $\overrightarrow{AO} = (\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$. Then $\overrightarrow{BO} = \overrightarrow{AO} - \overrightarrow{AB} = (-\vec{a} + \vec{b})/2$, and similarly $\overrightarrow{CO} = -(\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$ and $\overrightarrow{DO} = (\vec{a} - \vec{b})/2$ but magnitudes are the same. Adding vectors: $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{a} + (\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = 2\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. These give all seven requested expressions in terms of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

modelAnswer:
Let triangle ABC have position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, and let D, E be the midpoints of AB and AC respectively.

$D=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}$, $E=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}{2}$ (midpoint position-vector formula).

$\overrightarrow{DE}=E-D=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}{2}-\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}=\dfrac{\vec c-\vec b}{2}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BC}$

So $\overrightarrow{DE}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BC}$, hence $|DE|=\tfrac12|BC|$ (and DE is parallel to BC). This proves the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half the length of the third side.

$M=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec d}{2}$, $N=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec c}{2}$.

Since $AB\parallel DC$, $\vec c-\vec d=\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$ for some scalar $\lambda$.

$\overrightarrow{MN}=N-M=\dfrac{(\vec b-\vec a)+(\vec c-\vec d)}{2}=\dfrac{(\vec b-\vec a)+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)}{2}=\dfrac{1+\lambda}{2}(\vec b-\vec a)$

So $\overrightarrow{MN}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, hence **MN is parallel to both AB and DC**, the two parallel sides of the trapezium.
